templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Colon between independent clauses (second explains first)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a noun-phrase appositive that could rename the first sentence's last noun
items.passage: In 1989, a laborer dredging sand in the Philippine province of Laguna discovered a thin copper plate engraved with ______ acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE, the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1989, a laborer dredging sand in the Philippine province of Laguna discovered a thin copper plate engraved with text” is a complete sentence. The noun phrase “An acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE” describes “the inscription,” the subject of the second sentence, so it opens that sentence. A period after “text” marks the boundary between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “an acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE” seems to rename “text,” but the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” follows, so two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “engraved with text an acknowledgment” runs the first sentence into the noun phrase, and the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: Adding “which was” turns the noun phrase into a relative clause about the text, but the main clause “the inscription is the earliest known written document from the archipelago” is still joined to the first sentence by a comma alone, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, found in 1989, dated 900 CE, recording that a debt was cleared; the earliest known written document from the Philippines); real subject, details kept to what is well established, no person named. Band 7: 0fa289a7 (3.8) and 940ff6f7 move and menu: an 11-word noun-phrase opener (“An acknowledgment that a debt had been cleared in 900 CE”) reads as an appositive to “text” in A and D, and its own that-clause carries a finite verb (“had been cleared”), so the splice shows only at “the inscription,” 12 words past the blank, in a 41-word one-sentence run. Every wrong option fails on a rule (splice, fused, splice with added words); no semicolon option (a twin of the period) and no “, and” option.

band7.why: 0fa289a7 menu exactly (period, comma, none, comma plus “which was”); an 11-word noun-phrase opener whose own that-clause has a finite verb reads as an appositive to “text”, and the splice shows only at “the inscription”, 12 words past the blank, in a 41-word run.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a prepositional phrase
items.passage: The western underground orchid, found only in a few remnant patches of scrubland in Western Australia, completes its life cycle entirely below ground, even producing its flowers beneath the ______ chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize, the orchid obtains its nutrients from a fungus that is also connected to the roots of neighboring shrubs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The western underground orchid ... completes its life cycle entirely below ground, even producing its flowers beneath the soil” is a complete sentence. The next sentence has its own subject and verb, “the orchid obtains,” and opens with the prepositional phrase “Without chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize.” A period after “soil” separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: With a comma, “without chlorophyll with which to photosynthesize” reads as a tail of the first sentence, but “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Adding “and” doesn’t mark the boundary correctly. If “and” joins the two independent clauses, it needs a comma before it; if it links the without-phrase to the first sentence, the clause “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is joined to that sentence by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “beneath the soil without chlorophyll” runs the phrase into the first sentence, and the independent clause “the orchid obtains its nutrients” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (Rhizanthella gardneri, the Western Australian orchid that flowers underground and gets nutrients through a fungus shared with shrub roots); real subject, no researcher named. Band 6 by plan: a 6-word prepositional opener, the band-6 opener type (1b97cce9, 73a6603c), with clause 2's subject 7 words past the blank. Every wrong option fails on a rule; no semicolon option (twin) and no “, and” option.

fixes: C why_wrong now covers both readings of “and” (missing comma before a clause-joining “and”, or a comma splice)

band7.why: Band-6 S1_period: 6-word prepositional opener, clause 2's subject 7 words past the blank; two splice disguises plus a fused option, all rule failures.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before “instead,” comma after
items.passage: Fires were so frequent in Edo (present-day Tokyo) that residents called them the “flowers of Edo.” The city’s firefighters, whose hand-operated pumps were too feeble to extinguish major blazes, seldom attempted to put out burning ______ working ahead of the flames, they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The city’s firefighters ... seldom attempted to put out burning buildings” and “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” are both independent clauses, so a semicolon after “buildings” joins them. The adverb “instead” belongs to the second clause, which says what the firefighters did in place of putting out the fires, so the comma after “instead” sets it off from “working ahead of the flames.”

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “working ahead of the flames” runs into the first clause, and the independent clause “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: A comma after “buildings” makes “working ahead of the flames” a tail of the first clause, so the independent clause “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” is joined to the first by commas alone.

C.why_wrong: Commas around “instead” can’t join two independent clauses; the first clause and “they demolished the wooden houses in a fire’s path” are still joined by commas alone.

items.notes: Subject: history (firefighting in Edo: weak hand pumps, houses pulled down to stop a fire's spread; the saying that fires were the flowers of Edo); real subject, no person named. Band 6 by plan: a9e5b788 (3.5) menu, two options dropping the adverb, with a 5-word participial phrase after the adverb so clause 2's subject arrives 6 words past the blank. Every option that has “instead” puts a comma after it; no option puts it at the end of clause 1, so nothing fails on meaning alone; no period option (“buildings. Instead,” would be a twin).

review.note: Edo appears in FSS w2b2 (sangaku) only as a period name; different subject.

band7.why: a9e5b788 band-6 shape: semicolon plus “instead,” with a 5-word participial phrase before clause 2's subject; every option with the adverb puts a comma after it, so nothing fails on meaning alone.

items.subtype: Adverb closing a dash supplement, then a semicolon joining the clauses (“, respectively;”)
items.passage: In Hindustani classical music, the tabla comprises two drums of contrasting dimensions—a narrow wooden treble drum and a broader metal or clay bass drum, played with the right and left ______ percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “dimensions” opens a supplementary element that names the two drums and says which hand plays each; “respectively” belongs to that element, so a comma separates it from “hands.” The semicolon after “respectively” then joins the first independent clause to the second, “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane.”

A.why_wrong: A comma after “respectively” can’t join the first independent clause to “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane”; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark after “respectively,” the first independent clause runs straight into the second, “percussionists vary the bass drum’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane,” so the two clauses are fused without punctuation.

D.why_wrong: The dash after “respectively” pairs with the dash after “dimensions” to close the supplementary element, so it can’t also mark the boundary between the two independent clauses; the clauses are left without a proper joining mark.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music: the tabla's narrow wooden right-hand treble drum and broader metal or clay left-hand bass drum); real subject, no person named. Band 7: e41018de, the band-7 S1_adverb item whose adverb closes a dash supplement before a clause join; the opening dash sits 19 words before the blank, so every option must be judged against a partner mark outside a 6-word window, and two levels (supplement, clause joint) are decided in one slot. Every wrong option fails on a rule (splice; fused; one dash asked to close the pair and join clauses); review replaced e41018de's “; respectively” decoy, which a safety check could read as wrong on meaning alone, with the band-7 recipe's fused `L, adv R` option, so no option is wrong by meaning alone, and “respectively” cannot be read as a subordinator.

fixes: option C “hands; respectively” (CB's e41018de decoy, wrong mainly on meaning) replaced by the fused “hands, respectively” so every wrong option breaks a punctuation rule
passage padded toward the models' median (42 to 47 words; models 45 and 48): “by pressing the heel of the hand against its membrane”

band7.why: e41018de shape: the adverb closes a dash supplement whose opening dash is 19 words before the blank, so the slot decides two levels (close the supplement or join the clauses); the closing-dash decoy is the trap. Review swapped the meaning-only “; respectively” for a fused option, which is the easiest decoy, but the decisive choice (semicolon against a dash that seems to close the pair) still needs the far partner mark.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a complex series, with a second slot inside the first item
items.passage: Steelpans, the percussion instruments that Trinidadian musicians fashioned from discarded oil drums in the 1940s, are organized in a steel orchestra by ______ the tenor pans, which carry the melody; in the middle, the guitar and cello pans, which supply rhythmic chords; and at the bottom, the bass pans, each constructed from an entire drum.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Steelpans ... are organized in a steel orchestra by range” is a complete clause, and what follows is a list of the groups, separated by semicolons because each item contains commas. A colon after “range” introduces that list, and the comma after “at the top” separates the first item’s position from the pans it names, as the commas after “in the middle” and “at the bottom” do in the later items.

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t introduce a list whose items are separated by semicolons; after “range,” the list of groups needs a colon to set it up.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “at the top, the tenor pans, which carry the melody” is the first item of a list, not a clause.

D.why_wrong: With no colon, “at the top” runs into the clause (“organized in a steel orchestra by range at the top”), and nothing introduces the list of groups that follows.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music: steel orchestra sections, tenor, guitar and cello, and bass pans; pans made from oil drums in 1940s Trinidad); real subject, no person named. Band 6: e7afd0a1 shape (a colon before a complex series plus the comma inside the first item), with the menu's colon-in-the-wrong-place option replaced by a semicolon so that every wrong option fails on a plain rule (no colon to introduce the list, semicolon before a non-clause). No lone dash option (it would be a twin of the colon).

review.note: “discarded oil drums” also appears in FSS w2b4 (Haitian drum sculpture); shared phrase, different subject.

band7.why: e7afd0a1 band-6 shape: colon before a complex series with a second slot inside item 1; all wrong options plain rule failures.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase whose relative clause and so-that clause hold finite verbs
items.passage: Most diamonds form more than 150 kilometers below Earth’s surface, far deeper than any mine has ever reached. The gems are carried upward by a rare and violent type of ______ kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle through narrow pipes so quickly that the diamonds reach the surface before they can turn into graphite.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The gems are carried upward by a rare and violent type of volcanism” is a complete clause that announces something, and the noun phrase “kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma ... before they can turn into graphite” names that type of volcanism. A colon after “volcanism” introduces this explanation.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle through narrow pipes so quickly that the diamonds reach the surface before they can turn into graphite” has no main verb (“drive” belongs to the which-clause and “reach” to the that-clause), so it isn’t a clause.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “type of volcanism kimberlite eruptions” runs the noun phrase into the clause, and nothing marks it as the explanation of what that type of volcanism is.

D.why_wrong: With a period, “Kimberlite eruptions, which drive magma from the mantle ... before they can turn into graphite” would stand alone as a sentence, but all of its verbs are inside the which-clause, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology: diamonds form deep in the mantle and reach the surface in rare, fast kimberlite eruptions, which keep them from turning into graphite); standard textbook account, no researcher or institution named. Replaced in review: the draft's subject (biological ice nucleators in snowfall from several continents) is already served by boundaries.S4_object.easy.w1b1_20. Adjacent but distinct: boundaries.S4_restrictive.hard.w1b2_07 mentions a diamond only as the carrier of a ringwoodite sample (water in the mantle). Band 7: f30a478e menu (colon, semicolon, none, period) and the e9aee0d8 move: clause 1 ends on an announcing phrase (“a rare and violent type of volcanism”), and the noun phrase after the colon holds a which-clause and a so-that clause with finite verbs (“drive”, “reach”, “can turn”), so the semicolon and period versions read like sentences until the end, 25 words past the blank. No bare comma (it would read as a legal appositive) and no lone dash (twin).

fixes: new subject (kimberlite eruptions carrying diamonds): the draft's biological ice nucleators in snowfall duplicate served item boundaries.S4_object.easy.w1b1_20; same S2_colon build, menu, key letter and band-7 move

band7.why: Rewritten on the f30a478e menu with the e9aee0d8 move: an announcing clause (“a rare and violent type of volcanism”) and a noun phrase whose which-clause and so-that clause carry finite verbs (“drive”, “reach”, “can turn”), so the semicolon and period versions look like sentences until the end, 25 words past the blank; no comma or dash twin.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a title and a name, or between the name and its verb
items.passage: Between the eighth and tenth centuries, visitors to Sigiriya, a rock fortress in Sri Lanka, inscribed hundreds of poems on a polished wall. In 1956, after years spent deciphering the faded, often overlapping lines, Sri Lankan ______ published translations of 685 of these verses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Senarath Paranavithana” identifies which Sri Lankan epigraphist is meant, so it is essential information and isn’t set off from the title “Sri Lankan epigraphist” with punctuation. No punctuation is needed after the name either, because “Sri Lankan epigraphist Senarath Paranavithana” is the subject of the verb “published.”

A.why_wrong: Commas around “Senarath Paranavithana” treat the name as extra information, but with no article before the title, the name is essential; it identifies the epigraphist, so it shouldn’t be set off.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Paranavithana” separates the subject, “Sri Lankan epigraphist Senarath Paranavithana,” from its verb, “published.”

C.why_wrong: The comma after “epigraphist” separates the title from the essential name that identifies it, and it is left without a partner before the verb.

items.notes: Subject: literature and history (the Sigiri graffiti, verses visitors wrote on Sigiriya's Mirror Wall between the eighth and tenth centuries, translated by Senarath Paranavithana in 1956, many addressed to the fresco maidens); real person with his real, well-known work, kept from recall. Band 7: 5aae2475 and 6d4b2e1e menu (all four comma placements around title plus name), two slots under two rules (restrictive appositive, subject-verb), placed after an 11-word introductory element full of commas that ends in a comma (“In 1956, after years spent deciphering the faded, often overlapping lines,”), as in b4_07, so a comma pair around the name looks natural; the article-less title (“Sri Lankan epigraphist”) rules it out. Local by nature, as every S4_restrictive item is.

review.note: Real person and real work kept as written (Paranavithana's 1956 Sigiri Graffiti, 685 verses, a standard account); no search, per the brief. The surname is also romanized “Paranavitana” in English scholarship; both forms are in use, left unchanged and unverified.

band7.why: Matches the 5aae2475 and 6d4b2e1e menu exactly (all four comma placements around title plus name), two rules in one slot, after an 11-word comma-laden opener that makes a comma pair look natural; local by nature, as every S4_restrictive item is at every band.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a title and a name
items.passage: Tengenenge, a stone sculpture community in northern Zimbabwe, was founded in 1966 by tobacco ______ Tom Blomefield, who, after international sanctions crippled his business, invited the workers on his farm to try carving the serpentine stone found there.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Tom Blomefield” is essential information that identifies the “tobacco farmer” who founded Tengenenge, so no punctuation should separate the title from the name. The comma after “Blomefield” begins the nonessential who-clause; it doesn’t pair with anything before the name.

A.why_wrong: A comma after “farmer” sets off the name as if it were extra information, but with no article before “tobacco farmer,” the name is essential, and the comma after “Blomefield” belongs to the who-clause, not to a pair around the name.

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “Tengenenge ... was founded in 1966 by tobacco farmer” is incomplete without the name it introduces.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon can’t separate a title from the name it identifies; neither side of it is an independent clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Tengenenge sculpture community, founded in 1966 on Tom Blomefield's tobacco farm when sanctions hurt tobacco, serpentine stone); real person and the standard account of the founding, kept from recall and general. Band 6: 3.11 (594b4a94) menu with the 3.30 trap: the comma after the name, already in the passage for the who-clause, makes A look like a polite comma pair; the article-less title rules it out.

review.note: Tom Blomefield founding Tengenenge in 1966 on his tobacco farm after sanctions is the standard account and is kept general; no search, per the brief.

band7.why: 594b4a94 menu with the 80aa7690 trap (the who-clause comma after the name invites a false pair); article-less title rules it out.

items.subtype: Dash pair around a nonrestrictive relative clause inside a restrictive one; the blank opens the pair
items.passage: Legally, any licensed fisher may set lobster traps almost anywhere along Maine’s coastline. In practice, though, newcomers seldom last long in territories that a harbor’s established ______ enforce their claims by severing the lines of an outsider’s traps—consider their exclusive domain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “traps” closes a supplementary element, so a matching dash must open it. Placed after “lobstermen,” the dash sets off “who enforce their claims by severing the lines of an outsider’s traps,” an element that can be removed without breaking the sentence, which would still say that newcomers seldom last long in territories the established lobstermen consider their own.

B.why_wrong: A comma can’t open a supplementary element that a dash closes; the marks around “who enforce their claims by severing the lines of an outsider’s traps” must match.

C.why_wrong: Without a mark before “who,” the dash after “traps” has no partner, so the supplementary element is closed but never opened.

D.why_wrong: The dash after “who” separates the relative pronoun from its own verb, “enforce,” and the pair of dashes no longer encloses an element that could be removed.

items.notes: Subject: social science (informal territories of Maine's lobster harbor gangs, enforced by cutting intruders' trap lines; the anthropology of the Maine lobster fishery); real subject, kept general, no researcher named. Band 6: 626a1642 (3.34) menu exactly, with a different frame: the dash pair sits inside a restrictive that-clause (“territories that ... consider their exclusive domain”), and the closing dash is 11 words after the blank.

band7.why: 626a1642 menu, dash pair inside a restrictive that-clause with the closing dash 11 words past the blank.

items.subtype: Colon between independent clauses; the second explains the first and opens with a participial phrase
items.passage: In suminagashi, a Japanese technique for decorating paper with floating ink, a practitioner exercises only limited control over the ______ having touched an ink-laden brush to a water-filled tray, the artist can influence the concentric rings of pigment only by blowing on them or fanning them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In suminagashi ... a practitioner exercises only limited control over the design” and “the artist can influence the concentric rings of pigment only by blowing on them or fanning them” are both independent clauses, and the second explains the first: it shows how limited that control is. A colon after “design” joins the clauses and introduces this explanation.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “having touched an ink-laden brush to a water-filled tray” reads as a tail of the first clause, but “the artist can influence the concentric rings of pigment” is a second independent clause, so the two are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the participial phrase runs into the first clause, and the independent clause “the artist can influence the concentric rings of pigment” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can’t join these two long independent clauses, and “and” would present the second clause as an added fact rather than as the explanation of the artist’s limited control.

items.notes: Subject: arts (suminagashi, Japanese ink marbling: ink floated on water, moved by breath or fanning before paper is laid on it); real subject, no person named. Band 7: 6fac7f45 move: clause 1 announces (“only limited control over the design”), clause 2 explains and opens with a 9-word perfect-participle phrase that reads as a legal trailing modifier of clause 1 in A and B until “the artist can influence,” 10 words past the blank. The official band-7 relation-word decoys (“while”, “, while”) are left out because a subordinator makes a grammatical sentence; the 3.16 “and,” decoy takes their place, so every wrong option fails on a rule. No semicolon or period option (both would be legal twins).

band7.why: bb4557cf menu exactly (comma, none, “and,”, colon), so the official band-7 relation-word decoy is present as “and,” rather than “while”; clause 1 announces (“only limited control”), clause 2 opens with a 9-word perfect-participle phrase that reads as a trailing modifier until “the artist can influence”, 10 words past the blank.

items.subtype: Closing comma of an appositive that contains its own comma-set appositive
items.passage: Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped granite tower built in Gyeongju, the capital of the Silla kingdom, during the reign of Queen Seondeok in the seventh ______ is frequently identified as the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “Cheomseongdae” opens a supplementary element that describes the tower, and that element runs through “in the seventh century”; the commas around “the capital of the Silla kingdom” are a smaller pair inside it. A comma after “century” closes the larger element, pairing with the comma after “Cheomseongdae,” so the sentence reads “Cheomseongdae ... is frequently identified as the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia.”

A.why_wrong: With no comma after “century,” the supplementary element opened after “Cheomseongdae” is never closed, and the subject runs straight into the verb “is.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped granite tower ... in the seventh century” has no verb of its own.

C.why_wrong: A dash can’t close a supplementary element that a comma opened after “Cheomseongdae”; the marks must match.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (Cheomseongdae, the Silla-period granite tower in Gyeongju from Queen Seondeok's reign, often called East Asia's oldest surviving observatory); real subject, standard facts. Band 6: the S3_comma_pair hard cell has only one official (3.12, band 6), and the comma-pair shape whose partner sits far back is 2.14's; here the partner is 22 words back and a second comma pair nested inside the element (“the capital of the Silla kingdom”) tempts a student to think the element already closed. Every wrong option fails on a rule.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6: the partner comma is 22 words back with a nested comma pair inside the element.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: From 1866 until 1984, a network of underground tubes connected post offices throughout Paris, carrying messages in canisters propelled by compressed air. Messages sent this way usually arrived within a few ______ Parisians came to rely on these “petits bleus,” named for their blue paper, for urgent notes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Messages sent this way usually arrived within a few hours” is an independent clause, and so is the clause that follows, which begins “Parisians came to rely on these” and ends “for urgent notes.” A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two independent clauses of this length, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two independent clauses; without a conjunction, the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Paris pneumatic post, 1866 to 1984, its blue message forms called petits bleus); real subject, no person named. Medium: the standard 8-of-11 menu (and / , and / , / none); no semicolon or period option (a twin of the key).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: Pearlfish, slender, eel-like fish that shelter inside living sea cucumbers after entering tail first through an opening at the host’s rear, typically leave their hosts at night to hunt small ______ a few species, the fish remain permanently inside and feed on the sea cucumber’s reproductive organs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Pearlfish ... typically leave their hosts at night to hunt small crustaceans” is a complete sentence. “In a few species” is an introductory phrase that begins the next sentence, whose subject and verb are “the fish remain.” A period after “crustaceans” marks the boundary between the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “in a few species” seems to belong to the first sentence, but “the fish remain permanently inside and feed on the sea cucumber’s reproductive organs” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can’t join these two independent clauses (“Pearlfish ... typically leave their hosts” and “the fish remain permanently inside”).

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “small crustaceans in a few species” runs the introductory phrase into the first sentence, and the independent clause “the fish remain permanently inside” is then joined to it by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (pearlfish, Carapidae, sheltering in sea cucumbers; most hunt small crustaceans at night, a few species live permanently inside and eat the host's gonads); real subject, no researcher named. Medium: a 4-word prepositional opener (2.7, 2.9 type), menu of 2.7 and 2.27 (period / comma / none / and). No semicolon option (twin) and no “, and” option (legal).

items.subtype: Closing comma of an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Each pyrosome, a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as ______ drifts through warm seas worldwide, propelled by a gentle jet that its members create by pumping seawater through the colony’s wall.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “pyrosome” opens a supplementary element, “a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as zooids,” that describes the pyrosome. A comma after “zooids” closes that element, pairing with the first comma, so the main clause reads “Each pyrosome ... drifts through warm seas worldwide.”

B.why_wrong: Without a comma after “zooids,” the supplementary element opened by the comma after “pyrosome” is never closed.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Each pyrosome, a hollow tube made up of thousands of genetically identical animals known as zooids” has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: A dash can’t close a supplementary element that a comma opened; the marks around the description of the pyrosome must match.

items.notes: Subject: science (pyrosomes, colonial tunicates made of budded, genetically identical zooids that pump water to move the colony); real subject, no researcher named. Medium: 2.1 shape and menu (comma / none / semicolon / dash); the partner comma is 13 words back.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: At the hydrothermal field of Dallol, which lies below sea level in Ethiopia’s Danakil Depression, one of the hottest regions on Earth, scalding, acidic water percolates up through thick salt deposits and pools at the ______ the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “scalding, acidic water percolates up through thick salt deposits and pools at the surface” is the main clause, and “staining the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize” is a participial phrase that describes what the water does as it collects. A comma correctly separates the main clause from this supplementary phrase.

A.why_wrong: With a period, “Staining the ground in vivid shades of yellow, green, and orange as dissolved minerals crystallize” would stand alone as a sentence, but it has no subject or main verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the participial phrase beginning “staining the ground” isn’t a clause.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the participial phrase runs into the main clause and seems to describe “the surface” rather than the water; a comma is needed before this supplementary phrase.

items.notes: Subject: science (the Dallol hydrothermal field in Ethiopia's Danakil Depression, below sea level, hot acidic brine, yellow, green and orange mineral deposits); real subject, no figures, no person named. Medium: 2.4 and 2.26 menu (period / comma / semicolon / none) with an -ing tail after a long one-sentence run.

items.subtype: Closing dash of a dash pair between subject and verb
items.passage: Rosemaling—a style of decorative painting that flourished in the rural valleys of Norway from about 1750 to ______ covered wooden chests, bowls, and walls with swirling scrolls and stylized flowers, and Norwegian immigrants later brought it to the United States.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “Rosemaling” opens a supplementary element that defines the term, “a style of decorative painting that flourished in the rural valleys of Norway from about 1750 to 1850.” A dash after “1850” closes that element, pairing with the first dash, so the main clause reads “Rosemaling ... covered wooden chests, bowls, and walls with swirling scrolls and stylized flowers.”

A.why_wrong: A comma can’t close a supplementary element that a dash opened; the marks around the definition of rosemaling must match.

B.why_wrong: Without a mark after “1850,” the supplementary element opened by the dash after “Rosemaling” is never closed.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the words before the blank (“Rosemaling” and the definition after it) have no main verb, so they aren’t a clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts (rosemaling, Norwegian decorative folk painting of about 1750 to 1850 on chests, bowls and walls, carried to the United States by immigrants); real subject, no person named. Medium: 2.13 menu (semicolon / none / comma / dash) with the partner dash 17 words back.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before “however,” comma after
items.passage: After their expulsion from Spain in 1492, many Sephardic Jews settled in the Ottoman Empire, where their Spanish evolved into Ladino. For centuries, Ladino thrived in cities such as Salonica, supporting newspapers and a rich tradition of ______ the language declined sharply in the twentieth century as communities were destroyed or dispersed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “For centuries, Ladino thrived in cities such as Salonica, supporting newspapers and a rich tradition of ballads” and “the language declined sharply in the twentieth century as communities were destroyed or dispersed” are both independent clauses, so a semicolon after “ballads” joins them. The adverb “however” begins the second clause, which contrasts with the first, and is followed by a comma.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “however” can’t join two independent clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark before “however,” the adverb runs into the first clause, and the two independent clauses are then joined by a comma alone.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together: “a rich tradition of ballads the language declined sharply.”

items.notes: Subject: language (Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish of Sephardic Jews in Ottoman cities such as Salonica, with its newspapers and ballads, and its twentieth-century decline); real subject, no person named. Replaced a Baybayin draft that repeated item 01's early-Philippine-writing theme. Medium: 2.8 shape (adverb opens clause 2) with the a9e5b788 drop-the-adverb option; every option that has “however” puts a comma after it, so it can’t read as “in whatever way”; no “, however;” option (it would fail only on meaning) and no period option (twin).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: Flying fish inhabit tropical and subtropical oceans around the world. To escape predators such as tuna, they leap out of the water and glide ______ the waves on stiff, winglike fins, sometimes traveling more than 50 meters in a single flight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: No punctuation is needed between the preposition “over” and its object, “the waves.” Together they tell where the fish glide.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “To escape predators such as tuna, they leap out of the water and glide over” is incomplete; the preposition needs its object.

B.why_wrong: A comma shouldn’t separate the preposition “over” from its object, “the waves.”

C.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t come between the preposition and its object, and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

items.notes: Subject: science (flying fish: leaping from the water and gliding on enlarged, winglike fins to escape predators, glides of 50 meters or more); standard natural history, no researcher named. Replaced in review: the draft's subject (sand cats) is an official Text Structure and Purpose item (190857f0). Easy: preposition plus object, menu of colon, comma, dash and none (1.5, 1.9).

fixes: new subject (flying fish): the draft's sand cat is official Text Structure and Purpose item 190857f0; same preposition-object build, menu and key letter

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Launched by the government of the Indian state of Kerala in 1998, Kudumbashree organizes women into small neighborhood groups. Members pool their savings, lend money to one another, and ______ small businesses such as tailoring shops, farms, and cafés.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “start” and its object, “small businesses,” form the last of the three actions listed for the members, so no punctuation should come between them.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “Members pool their savings, lend money to one another, and start” is incomplete; the verb needs its object.

B.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t separate the verb “start” from its object, “small businesses,” and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

D.why_wrong: A comma between “start” and “small businesses” splits the verb from its object; no punctuation belongs there.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Kudumbashree, Kerala's women's neighborhood-group network launched by the state government in 1998: savings, loans, small enterprises); real subject, no person named. Easy: verb plus object inside a three-part series of verb phrases; the blank is after the verb of item 3, not at a series comma.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In Basque bertsolaritza, singers improvise verses on topics given to them moments earlier. The verses must follow strict rules of rhyme and ______ skilled singers compose them almost instantly, often before large crowds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The verses must follow strict rules of rhyme and meter” and “skilled singers compose them almost instantly” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast between the strict rules and the singers’ speed.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two independent clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can’t join the two independent clauses; the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: literature (bertsolaritza, Basque improvised sung verse on topics set just before performing, with strict rhyme and meter); real subject, no person named. Easy: the 1.2 and 1.27 menu (, but / but / , / none). The “and” before the blank is inside clause 1 (“rhyme and meter”), not a joining word.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything ______ vakhs, or short mystical verses, have survived for more than six centuries, preserved by devotees who memorized and recited them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything down” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause, whose subject and verb are “her vakhs ... have survived.” A comma after “down” separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the clause beginning “Although” is dependent, so it can’t stand on one side of a semicolon.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, the introductory clause runs into the main clause (“written anything down her vakhs”); a comma is needed after an introductory clause like this one.

D.why_wrong: With a period, “Although the fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded is not known to have written anything down” would stand alone as a sentence, but it is a dependent clause, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Lal Ded, or Lalleshwari, fourteenth-century Kashmiri mystic poet whose vakhs survived through oral recitation); real subject. Easy: Although-clause (1.8) with the menu semicolon / comma / none / period.

items.subtype: Indirect question inside a statement: statement word order and a period
items.passage: At Lothal, an Indus Valley city in western India, archaeologists uncovered a large rectangular basin lined with fired bricks. Some believe boats docked there, while others argue that it functioned as a reservoir; scholars still debate what purpose ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The last clause is a statement about what scholars debate, and “what purpose the basin served” is an indirect question within it. An indirect question takes statement word order, with the subject “the basin” before the verb “served,” and the sentence ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: This choice uses the word order and question mark of a direct question, but the sentence is a statement about what scholars debate, so the indirect question needs statement order and a period.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for an indirect question, but the sentence as a whole is a statement, so it should end with a period, not a question mark.

C.why_wrong: The inverted word order (“did the basin serve”) belongs to a direct question; inside a statement, the indirect question needs statement order: “the basin served.”

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the brick basin at Lothal, read as a dockyard by some and a reservoir by others); real debate, no person named. Easy: the 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark (1.7, 1.24), with the blank ending the passage as in 1.24.

review.note: Shares the Indus civilization with official Inferences item 4e9afd7a but not its subject (the Lothal basin debate); acceptable.

items.subtype: Comma between items of a simple series (blank after item 1)
items.passage: Hong Kong’s Octopus card, introduced in 1997, was among the first contactless payment cards in widespread use. Commuters first used it to pay train and bus fares, but today it also pays for groceries at convenience ______ snacks from vending machines, and parking at meters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things the card pays for: “groceries at convenience stores,” “snacks from vending machines,” and “parking at meters.” A comma after “stores” separates the first item from the second, just as the comma after “machines” separates the second from the third.

A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate the items in a list only when the items themselves contain commas; these items don’t, so a comma is needed.

C.why_wrong: A colon can’t be used between two items in a list; “snacks from vending machines” is the second item, not an explanation of the first.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the first and second items run together (“convenience stores snacks”).

items.notes: Subject: social science (Hong Kong's Octopus card, 1997, an early contactless payment card later used beyond transit); real subject. Easy: simple series with the blank after item 1, as in 1.3, 1.12 and 1.25, never at the optional serial-comma slot.

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that-clause (relative pronoun needed)
items.passage: For years, home internet access in Cuba was rare and costly. Many Cubans instead relied on el paquete semanal (“the weekly package”), a bundle of digital ______ travels from home to home each week on portable hard drives, bringing films, TV shows, music, and magazines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “that travels from home to home each week on portable hard drives” tells which bundle of digital files is meant, so it is essential and isn’t set off with punctuation. The relative pronoun “that” is needed as the clause’s subject; without it, the verb “travels” has nothing to attach to.

A.why_wrong: A dash shouldn’t separate “files” from the essential clause beginning “that travels,” and nothing else in the sentence pairs with it.

B.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “travels” has no subject of its own, so “a bundle of digital files travels from home to home” can’t fit into the sentence.

D.why_wrong: A comma shouldn’t come before “that” here: the clause it begins is essential to the meaning of “a bundle of digital files,” and essential relative clauses aren’t set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science (el paquete semanal, Cuba's weekly offline media collection carried on hard drives); real subject, no person named. Easy: 1.29 shape (the relative pronoun is the clause's subject, so the no-that option is ungrammatical) with a stray-dash option in place of 1.29's bare comma.
